name: Pork Belly Okonomiyaki (Japanese Savoury Pancakes)
why: Late-August cabbage at its sweetest meets one of Japan's best street-food techniques — a savoury pancake that's essentially a 30-minute, one-pan frittata with a golden pork belly base. New technique, big flavour, zero fuss.
author: Henry
ingredients: 100g cooked pork belly, thinly sliced into bite-sized pieces
1 tbsp vegetable oil (plus a little extra for basting)
okonomi sauce (Japanese brown sauce), to serve (optional)

steps: Crack the egg into a large bowl, tip in the flour, bouillon powder and 100ml water, and mix well into a smooth batter.
Stir the shredded cabbage into the batter and season well with salt and black pepper — the mix will look loose and runny, that's correct.
Whisk the Worcestershire sauce, ketchup and caster sugar in a small bowl to make a quick glaze; season lightly.
Shred the nori sheet, slice the spring onions, and get the mayo and bonito flakes ready for topping.
Heat the oil in a small, deep frying pan or skillet (about 19cm) over medium heat.
Add the pork belly slices and fry for 4-5 minutes until golden and the fat has rendered.
Pour the cabbage batter over the pork, stir everything together, and fry for 5 minutes until dark brown underneath and semi-cooked in the middle.
Flip the pancake (a wide, flat spatula helps) and cook for a further 5 minutes until golden-brown on the other side and cooked right through.
Transfer the okonomiyaki to a plate — split in half if it's big enough, or make two smaller rounds.
Glaze with the Worcestershire-ketchup sauce, then drizzle with mayonnaise (use a skewer to zig-zag it on for that street-stall look).
Top with shredded nori, sliced spring onions and a scatter of bonito flakes if using, and serve straight away.

pro_tips: The deep skillet is doing real work: with a 19cm pan and a lid, you can baste the tall edges with oil while the pancake sets, so it crisps up all the way round instead of just on the flat faces — that's the difference between home and street-stall okonomiyaki.

Okonomiyaki is the ultimate leftover vehicle — swap the pork belly for leftover roast chicken, prawns or firm tofu, and a handful of tenkasu (tempura crisps) folded into the batter adds that airy, restaurant-level crunch.
